title: Dharma at the lake
hookLine: one brother may live: Yudhishthira chooses Nakula, and the yaksha shows who he really is

cards: The questions are over, and the yaksha is satisfied. One of your brothers may live, he says. Choose.
On the shore lie four of them. Bhima, whose strength the family leans on. Arjuna, the archer they'll need in any war to come.
And the twins, Nakula and Sahadeva. Yudhishthira looks at them all, one by one, for a long moment. Then he names one, and the yaksha asks him why.

teach.b: Let Nakula live, Yudhishthira says. Why him? Why not Bhima, so strong, or Arjuna, whom you all depend on?
Yudhishthira answers: my father had two wives, Kunti and Madri. I am Kunti's son, and I'm alive.

teach.h: A LIVING SON FOR MADRI TOO.
teach.b: Let Madri have a living son too. He passes over the brothers who could win him a war, and chooses the one who keeps the family fair. The yaksha is delighted.
Because you hold not being cruel higher than gain or pleasure, he says, let all four of your brothers live. And they stand up, as if from sleep. Then the stranger shows his face.

teach.h: THE YAKSHA IS DHARMA, HIS FATHER.
teach.b: He is Dharma himself, Yudhishthira's own father, and the deer that ran off with the fire-sticks was Dharma too. Here's the teaching, and it's one of the epic's biggest.
The Sanskrit word is anrishamsya: not being cruel, keeping your heart open to the person a cold calculation would leave out.
The Mahabharata ranks it among the highest dharma, and this is the moment that shows why Yudhishthira is called Dharmaraja, the king of dharma. Dharma here isn't a rulebook.
It's the moment the clever move and the kind move split, and you take the kind one.
Dharma grants him gifts: the fire-sticks back, a year in hiding where no one will know them, and a mind set on generosity, truth and self-discipline.
Today the same choice comes small: who gets picked, who gets the bigger share, whose turn it is. Dharma's question isn't who helps me most. It's who would be left out.

how: Yudhishthira's choice of Nakula comes after the last of the questions, and the revelation that the yaksha was Dharma closes the story of the lake.

o: the god Dharma, Yudhishthira's father, testing his son
the spirit of the lake, punished for its riddles
the sage who taught the Pandavas in the forest

games.q: how the lake ends — tap the pairs.
p: should have a living son too

s: Yudhishthira chose Bhima because he was strongest
he chose Nakula, so that Madri, like Kunti, would have a living son.
the yaksha was Dharma, Yudhishthira's own father
he came to see his son and to test him.
the deer that took the fire-sticks was part of the test
Dharma says the deer was him too.

games.q: you're Yudhishthira. one brother may live. a war may be coming. who do you choose?
o: Bhima, whose strength protects you all.
games.why: Nakula, so both his father's wives have a living son. because he holds not being cruel above gain, the yaksha, Dharma himself, lets all four live.

practice: Bring to mind a group you belong to, a family, a team, a circle of friends, and look for the person in it who is easiest to overlook, the one without a loud voice on their side.
Hold them in mind the way Yudhishthira holds Madri's sons in mind, and with each breath wish them well. If you pray, you can bring them into your prayer.

wordCard.voice: Dharma, the god who stood at the lake all along, revealed at last as Yudhishthira's own father. A test by a lake that ends with a fair choice, and four brothers alive. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit: dharma, the right way; here also Dharma, the god who is Yudhishthira's father.

carryVoice: Your line: dharma puts non-cruelty above gain. A living son for each mother, and four brothers standing. Day eight hundred six, done.

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Vana Parva (Aranyaka Parva), the end of the episode of the Yaksha's questions: the choice of Nakula; the brothers restored; the yaksha revealed as Dharma; the boons
